title: A Nice Worksheet
author: Dylan Kane
summary: In an 'annual-ish' post defending the humble worksheet, Dylan Kane pushes back against the reflex assumption that putting math problems on paper is inherently boring or regressive compared to other activity formats. He walks through a specific worksheet on combining like terms, used early in an expressions unit, and breaks down five deliberate design choices that made it effective: it starts simple and builds difficulty gradually to build student confidence; it's short enough (18 quick problems, four minutes of work) to sustain focus without dragging; it deliberately targets three specific, common misconceptions about combining like terms (missing coefficients on x/-x, wrongly combining variable and constant terms, and sign errors with negatives); each problem is a small variation on the last, following variation theory, which makes repetitive practice both more engaging for confident students and more accessible for less-confident ones; and it's genuinely quick to create, taking only a few minutes. Kane's underlying argument is that the worth of a worksheet depends entirely on whether it serves genuine mathematical thinking and surfaces misconceptions for discussion, not on the format itself.
points: Kane's reframe -- the problem isn't the worksheet format, it's whether a given worksheet facilitates thinking and surfaces misconceptions -- directly counters a common progressive-vs-traditional framing that judges activities by surface features rather than the thinking they produce.

His targeting of three specific, named misconceptions (missing coefficient on x/-x, combining variable and constant terms, sign errors with negatives) shows the worksheet was designed around known error patterns, not just generic practice problems.

The variation-theory design principle -- each problem a small variation on the last -- is explicitly credited with a dual benefit: making repetitive practice feel less tedious for confident students while making it more accessible for less-confident ones via visible connections between problems.

His closing practical note -- that a well-designed worksheet like this takes 'a few minutes' to create -- pushes back against any assumption that principled resource design necessarily requires large amounts of preparation time.
quotes: One important component of learning math is solving math problems. One way to facilitate this in a classroom is to put a bunch of math problems on a piece of paper, hand that paper to students, and have students solve the problems.
The goal of giving students math problems is to cause the students to think about mathematical ideas, and to surface ideas and misconceptions for further discussion with the rest of the class.
It starts simple and gets gradually harder. In general, students are happy to do things that make them feel confident and successful.
It targets a few common misconceptions. Three common mistakes students make with expressions are not knowing what to do with x and -x since there is no written coefficient.
Each problem is connected to the previous problem. This idea comes from variation theory, which you can read more about here if you like.
It’s also pretty easy to whip up. I can make one of these in a few minutes.
There’s more to math than worksheets, but a good worksheet is a helpful tool for practice, and to set students up to do harder math down the road.
